analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for the government to seize and keep people's property without proving a crime in court.
analysis.headline: Backed by a bipartisan group of eight senators, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, police and federal agencies can take cash, cars, and other property on suspicion it was connected to a crime, then keep it unless the owner proves in court it was innocent — and the government only has to show its case is more likely than not. This bill would flip that: agencies could no longer take property through paperwork alone; they would have to go through a federal court, prove their case with clear and convincing evidence, and in drug cases show the owner knowingly used the property in a crime. It would also give free lawyers to people who cannot afford one, require a judge to review cash seizures within 14 days, and send forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury's general fund instead of letting law enforcement agencies keep the money themselves.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners — especially cash-heavy small business owners, travelers, and low-income people who are targets of civil forfeiture but are often never charged with a crime — would keep their property unless the government proved in court that it was tied to an actual offense, with a higher evidentiary standard and appointed counsel for those who cannot afford a lawyer [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans nonjudicial (administrative) forfeiture entirely: no federal seizing agency could take property without judicial involvement, and only a U.S. district court could enter a forfeiture order [S2].

It raises the government's burden of proof from a mere 'preponderance of the evidence' to 'clear and convincing evidence,' and requires the government to show the owner used the property to facilitate an offense or knowingly let it be used — instead of the owner having to fight to prove innocence [S2].

It lets courts appoint a lawyer for people who cannot afford one or whose legal fees would exceed the value of the seized property — fixing a situation where fighting to get back a few thousand dollars can cost more than the property is worth [S2].

It shortens notice deadlines from 60 days to 7 days after seizure, shortens the government's window to act from 90 days to 30 days, and requires a court hearing within 14 days on property seized in structuring cases, with the property returned unless a judge finds probable cause [S2].

It narrows the structuring crime so that merely making cash deposits under the reporting threshold is not a crime unless done knowingly with funds from an illegitimate source — addressing cases where ordinary businesses have had their entire bank accounts seized over routine cash deposits [S2].

It redirects forfeiture proceeds away from the Justice Department's Assets Forfeiture Fund and into the Treasury's General Fund, removing the direct financial incentive for agencies to seize property and spend the proceeds themselves [S2].

It adds a proportionality check: courts must weigh the seriousness of the offense, the connection of the property to it, and the hardship to the owner and dependents before allowing a forfeiture [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal seizing agencies and state and local police departments that share in federal forfeiture proceeds would lose a major revenue stream, and law enforcement would face a higher evidentiary bar for taking assets from suspected trafficking operations [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies that keep seized property

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the government's standard to 'clear and convincing evidence' and requires proof of a substantial connection between property and offense, which law enforcement groups argue would make it harder to strip drug traffickers and criminal organizations of their proceeds and assets [S2].

By ending administrative forfeiture and moving proceeds to the Treasury General Fund, it eliminates the funding channel that has paid for law enforcement equipment, training, and operations at federal agencies and through shared proceeds to state and local police [S2].

A supporter would honestly acknowledge that forfeiture is one of the few tools that hits criminal enterprises where it hurts — their money — and some legitimate cases that succeed today would become harder to win under the new standard [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For property owners, the protections are substantial: the bill removes the ability of agencies to take property with no court involved, raises the evidentiary bar, provides counsel, and cuts the profit motive out of seizures. The cost is real but narrower — law enforcement loses revenue and some asset-forfeiture cases against traffickers become harder to prove. On balance the bill trades some enforcement efficiency for a large gain in due process for people who are frequently never charged with any crime.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the Fifth Amendment Integrity Restoration Act of 2024 in the Senate on December 12, 2024 [S1] [S4].

The bill was sponsored by Paul and cosponsored by a bipartisan group of seven senators: three Democrats (Cory Booker, Ron Wyden, Chris Van Hollen), three Republicans (Mike Lee, Mike Crapo, Cynthia Lummis), and one independent (Angus King) [S2] [S3].
On the day of introduction, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee — and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without ever leaving committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies and seizing offices keep the status quo: they continue to take property through administrative process, keep the evidentiary threshold low, and continue drawing forfeiture proceeds through the Justice Department's Assets Forfeiture Fund and shared payments to state and local police. Property owners whose assets are seized remain in the same legal position as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies keeping seizure powers

industries.industry: Federal and state/local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill ends administrative forfeiture, raises the proof standard, and — most financially significant — sends forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury General Fund instead of the Justice Department's Assets Forfeiture Fund, cutting off the revenue agencies keep and share with state and local police. Agencies' financial interest in retaining seized property runs directly against owners' interest in keeping it.

industries.industry: Defense bar and civil rights legal services
industries.note: The bill authorizes court-appointed counsel for owners who cannot afford representation or whose legal costs would exceed the property's value, creating a right to counsel in civil forfeiture claims [S2].
